name: Saifa
description: An advanced kata that emphasizes powerful closed-fist techniques and aggressive impact movements.
history: Saifa was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown, but they undoubtedly had ties to Crane Boxing. Goju-ryu is the only karate style that has Saifa in its curriculum. Saifa means something like 'destructive attacks,' but the name is more commonly used, for example, for completely different quans in Shaolin Kung Fu.
culturalSignificance: The kata is characterized by, among other things, the high number of striking techniques, which are naturally circular and executed without tension in the wrist, elbow, and shoulder. There is also only minimal use of the upper body muscles, so that the student learns to optimally use the impulse from the legs and pelvis during the stroke.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Saifa was introduced to Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Sensei Miyagi adopted Saifa as the third Goju kata after the two Gekisai forms.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: Within Goju-Ryu, Saifa has always remained an advanced kata.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Features
technicalFeatures.content: The kata is characterized by its use of circular strikes and release techniques.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: Most Goju subsystems maintain Saifa more or less identically.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/Systems
relationships.content: Saifa aligns with the Naha-te tradition and shares similarities with Southern Chinese movements.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Saifa is traditionally trained as a specialized kata for advanced students.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: The name Saifa reflects its focus on 'tearing and breaking'.
